beats.speaker: Sifu, The Wise
beats.text:
Nothing here was built badly. That is what makes it frightening.

Every shortcut in these walls was taken by someone sensible, under a deadline, intending to come back.

beats.speaker: Sifu, The Wise
beats.text: The Technical Debt King rules by accumulation. It never takes much. It simply never gives anything back, and it charges interest.

beats.title: Technical debt is a real debt
beats.body:
The metaphor is precise. You borrow speed now by doing something the quick way, and you repay it later with interest — every future change in that area costs more than it should have.

Some debt is deliberate and wise: ship now, fix after the deadline. Some is accidental: nobody knew the better way. Both accrue. Only the first is ever planned for.

beats.title: Debt you chose, debt that happened
beats.left_body:
“We know this belongs in a service. We are hardcoding it to make the demo, and we have a ticket to fix it.”

Recorded, estimated, visible. Repayable.
beats.right_body:
“We didn't know the framework had a built-in for this, so we wrote our own, badly.”

Found years later by someone who did know. Invisible until then.

beats.title: Maintenance is most of the work
beats.body:
Software spends far more of its life being changed than being written. Maintenance is not the tidying-up after the project — it is the project, for most of its duration.

It takes four shapes: corrective (fix what is broken), adaptive (keep up with a changed world), perfective (improve what works), and preventive (make future change cheaper). Only the first is an emergency, and it is the only one most teams schedule.

beats.title: Changing code you are afraid of
steps: Do not refactor first. Untested code plus a rewrite is two unknowns multiplied.
Put a test around the current behaviour — even the wrong behaviour. You are recording what is, not what should be.
Make the smallest change that delivers the value asked for. Resist the tour.
Refactor in a separate, behaviour-preserving step, with the tests still green.
Leave it better than you found it by a little, every time. A codebase is improved the way it was ruined: gradually.

beats.title: Two ways to pay it down
beats.bad:
“This module is a disaster. Give me six weeks and I'll replace it properly.”

Six weeks becomes five months. The old module keeps changing meanwhile. Nothing ships.
beats.good:
Put a seam in front of the old module. Route one small piece of its work to a new implementation. Then another. Then another.

The old one shrinks until it is gone.
beats.verdict: The second delivers value from the first week and can be abandoned at any point without loss. Big-bang rewrites fail because they must be completely finished before they are worth anything at all.

beats.question: Which is the best reason to refactor a working module?
options: The code style is out of date
A change you need to make is hard because of how it is structured
beats.explanation: Correct answer: the second. Refactoring is justified by a change it makes possible, not by taste. Rewriting working code for style alone spends real risk on no delivered value — and the code you have not touched has the one quality yours does not yet: years of proof that it works.

beats.speaker: Sifu, The Wise
beats.text:
The King will offer you the same bargain everyone else took. A little now, paid later.

You may accept it. Just never accept it silently — debt you wrote down is a plan, and debt you did not is a trap.

beats.taunt: Everyone takes the shortcut. I'm simply the one who keeps the ledger.
beats.text: The Technical Debt King waits among the ruins.
